title: Write it down the moment you hear it
source_document: Simply Psychology: ADHD and Working Memory (Apr 4, 2026); Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no studies tested the tip itself. The Simply Psychology page is labelled an AI-assisted draft with editorial spot review, and its studies are cited second-hand and not verified here.
text:
Recognize it when: you were told something or had a thought, meant to do it later, and it was gone within minutes.
Technique: capture it in one trusted place at once, instead of trusting your head to hold it.
How: 1. Pick one capture place you always have with you (one notes app or one small notebook).
2. Write it the moment it comes up, not in a minute. Three to five words is enough: who, what, by when.
3. If it has a date, save it as a task with a due date and a reminder.
4. Look at the list at a set time each day so captured items turn into actions.
Why it helps: new information can push out what you were holding, so the memory fails before you can act on it. Writing it down moves the job of remembering out of your head.
Try saying: If it matters, it goes in the note now.
If it does not work: use a voice memo if typing is too slow.

title: Calendar for fixed commitments, task list for everything else
source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026); Unattributed AI-generated search overview on ADHD calendars and reminders (user-collected)
source_citation: Practitioner source (coach blog) plus an unattributed AI-generated overview that cites commercial and social media pages. No studies cited for the tip. Use for ideas only.
text:
Recognize it when: appointments and deadlines are scattered across notes, memory and different apps, or your calendar is full of tasks you never do.
Technique: use the calendar only for things with a fixed date and time, and one task list for everything else.
How: 1. Put appointments, classes and deadlines with a set date on the calendar, so they are not left to memory.
2. Put things without a set time on one task list.
3. Leave 15 to 30 minutes between events for travel and for things that run over.
4. Once a week, look ahead far enough to start preparing for what is coming.
Why it helps: a calendar that shows only real commitments can be trusted, and gaps between events protect you from underestimating how long things take.
Try saying: Fixed time goes in the calendar. Everything else goes on the list.
If it does not work: start with just the next two weeks of fixed events.

title: Set two or three reminders, not one
source_document: Inflow: 8 ways to budget and pay bills on time with ADHD (Ash Fisher, Nov 22, 2021); MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026); Unattributed AI-generated search overview on ADHD calendars and reminders (user-collected)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no ADHD trials of this tip. MossyMind cites Gilbert (2015) and Gilbert et al. (2023) on external reminders in general-population samples; verify before quoting. The AI overview is low quality and was used only where the other two agree.
text:
Recognize it when: you set one reminder and it gets dismissed or ignored, or you are too busy to act when it goes off.
Technique: use two or three reminders at different times, and label them with the action.
How: 1. Set a heads-up alert well ahead: 1 to 2 hours before an event, or about a week and two days before a bill or deadline.
2. Set an action alert 15 to 30 minutes before, when you need to start moving.
3. Write the action in the label (Leave for dentist, Pay phone bill), not just the event name.
4. Add one cue you can see, such as a note by the door or a watch buzz.
Why it helps: a single alert is easy to dismiss. Studies of the general population found that setting external reminders improves follow-through, and there is no reason to save them for when you are already struggling.
Try saying: One alert is a suggestion. Two or three is a plan.
If it does not work: add one more reminder in a different place, such as a phone alarm plus a note.

title: Forget to check your planner? Attach it to something you already do
source_document: AuDHD Psychiatry: Habit Stacking for ADHD (Jun 9, 2025); Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner sources, no studies cited for the tip. The AuDHD Psychiatry page is a clinic's marketing blog (reviewed by a chartered psychologist). Habit stacking is also covered in the earlier habit-stacking chunk.
text:
Recognize it when: you have a planner or calendar but forget to open it, or you keep starting and stopping a planning routine.
Technique: attach a two-minute planner check to something you already do every day.
How: 1. Pick one daily anchor, such as making coffee, waiting for the kettle, or changing into pyjamas.
2. Decide the tiny action: open the calendar and read today and tomorrow, or write your top three priorities.
3. Put a visual cue where the anchor happens (the planner by the kettle, a sticky note on the mirror).
4. Tick it off on a tracker as a small reward.
5. If you miss days, simplify it and add a cue instead of starting over.
Why it helps: the anchor supplies the reminder, so you rely less on memory or willpower.
Try saying: After I make coffee, I check my calendar.
If it does not work: shrink the action to just opening the calendar, or move it to a different anchor.

title: Turn 'remember at 3 pm' into a cue you cannot miss
source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an app company's blog) that cites small studies: Altgassen et al. 2014 (25 adults with ADHD vs 25 controls) and 2019 (29 vs 24), and Gilbert 2015 (general population). Small samples; treat as clues, not settled facts. Not ADHD treatment.
text:
Recognize it when: you plan to do something at a set time (call at 3, take the form tomorrow) and the time passes without you remembering.
Technique: turn a time-based intention into a cue that shows up on its own.
How: 1. Instead of 'take the form to the pharmacy tomorrow', put the form on top of your keys tonight.
2. Instead of 'call the school at 2', set a phone alarm labelled with the action.
3. Put the item or the alarm where you will meet it at the right moment, such as the doormat or the front door.
4. When the cue appears, do the action, or move it to a new time on purpose.
Why it helps: small studies suggest adults with ADHD cope with cue-triggered reminders better than with remembering at a set time and no cue, though the groups were only about 25 to 30 people.
Try saying: I will not remember at 3. I will set something that finds me at 3.
If it does not work: add a second cue, such as a note on the door plus an alarm.

title: The 'I'll remember' trap: forgetting is not carelessness
source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026); Simply Psychology: ADHD and Working Memory (Apr 4, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner sources citing small studies and meta-analyses second-hand (for example a meta-analysis of 38 studies on working memory, and prospective memory studies with about 25 to 30 people per group). Not verified here. The Simply Psychology page is labelled an AI-assisted draft.
text:
Recognize it when: you tell yourself 'I'll remember' and then do not, or you think forgetting means you are careless or do not care.
Technique: treat forgetting as a memory-timing problem, and swap 'I'll remember' for a cue or a note.
How: 1. Notice the trap thought: I'll remember.
2. Ask what will bring this to mind at the right moment. If the answer is nothing, set something up.
3. Write it down, set an alarm, or put the item where you will see it.
4. Do this before you start the next thing, because a new task or an interruption can wipe out what you were holding.
Why it helps: remembering to do something later means holding an intention while other things compete for attention. Research suggests this is harder on average for adults with ADHD, and it does not mean you do not care.
Try saying: I am not careless. My memory needs a cue.
If it does not work: if forgetting is causing serious problems at work, with money or with health, talk to a clinician. Memory problems that are new, sudden or getting worse need prompt medical attention.

title: Put things where the action happens so they remind you
source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an app company's blog). The source says there is no trial of storage bins for ADHD, so treat these as experiments. Overlaps in part with the zones-and-homes chunk.
text:
Recognize it when: you put away things you need to act on (a library book, a bill, food) and forget them until it is too late.
Technique: put each item where the action happens, so the item itself reminds you.
How: 1. Put things that must leave the house on a spot by the door or on the doormat.
2. Keep bills and forms that need action in a clear tray, separate from mail you can recycle.
3. Put food that needs eating soon at eye level in the fridge.
4. Keep keys, wallet and charger in one bowl.
5. Keep the visible set small, so a pile of displayed things does not fade into the background.
Why it helps: a visible item prompts you at the right moment, so you depend less on remembering.
Try saying: If I need to act on it, it goes where I will see it.
If it does not work: try it with one item for a week and keep what works.

title: One daily list where unfinished tasks come back to you
source_document: MossyMind: Out of sight, out of mind with ADHD (Oct 15, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an app company's blog that sells a task app). No studies cited for this tip. Use the method, not the product.
text:
Recognize it when: tasks are spread across notes, apps and sticky notes, or yesterday's unfinished tasks scroll out of sight and get forgotten.
Technique: keep one daily list you open every day, where unfinished tasks come back to you.
How: 1. Choose one place for today's tasks and make sure everything you must act on shows up there.
2. Keep today short enough to read at a glance, about 3 to 5 tasks.
3. Let unfinished tasks carry forward to today instead of staying on a past date.
4. If a task has rolled over several days, decide: make it smaller, give it a firm date, park it, or delete it.
Why it helps: each extra place is one more thing to remember to check. A task should only leave your sight by being done, rescheduled on purpose, or deleted on purpose.
Try saying: One list, and nothing disappears unless I decide.
If it does not work: shrink today's list to three tasks.

title: A weekly review so nothing slips through
source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an ADHD coach's blog with a newsletter sign-up; draws on David Allen's Getting Things Done). No studies cited. The coach suggests trying it imperfectly for at least 8 weeks.
text:
Recognize it when: tasks and commitments keep slipping, you feel busy but not on top of things, or you are driven by whatever is loudest or latest.
Technique: a short weekly review of your inbox, task list, calendar and plan.
How: 1. Pick a set day and place, such as Thursday or Friday morning, so you go into the weekend ready.
2. Process: sort the week's loose papers, notes and missed messages into tasks, files or the bin.
3. Tasks: add new ones, tick off finished ones, and make sure each project has a next action.
4. Calendar: look at upcoming dates and add any preparation tasks.
5. Plan: choose where your time goes next week.
6. Reflect: what went well, and what is getting in the way?
7. Do not do the tasks during the review. Just collect and plan.
Why it helps: it replaces holding everything in your head with a regular check, and it builds confidence that you are not missing something.
Try saying: This is time to plan, not time to do.
If it does not work: do only part of it, and try it imperfectly for several weeks before you judge it.

title: Forgot to reply or follow up: track what you are waiting for
source_document: Marla Cummins: How This Weekly Habit Helps ADHD Adults Follow Through (updated Sep 29, 2026)
source_citation: Practitioner source (an ADHD coach's blog). No studies cited. The 'waiting for' list is from David Allen's Getting Things Done, as described by the coach.
text:
Recognize it when: you forgot to reply, you are waiting on someone and never followed up, or a message got buried.
Technique: reply at once if it takes two minutes or less, otherwise capture it, and track what you are waiting for with a follow-up date.
How: 1. If a reply takes two minutes or less, send it now.
2. Otherwise write it down as a task with a due date.
3. When you are waiting on someone, add a task such as 'text Sam if I have not heard back', dated a few days later.
4. Once a week, go through messages from the past week (email, texts, voicemail, chat apps).
5. Treat messages older than a week as a separate catch-up job.
Why it helps: 'waiting for' items are often overlooked because nothing reminds you of them. A dated task does the reminding.
Try saying: If I am waiting, I set a follow-up date.
If it does not work: if quick replies keep turning into long ones, write them down and answer in one set slot.

title: Pay bills on time: set it up once
source_document: Inflow: 8 ways to budget and pay bills on time with ADHD (Ash Fisher, Nov 22, 2021)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog based on the writer's own experience, published 2021. No studies cited. Auto-pay can overdraw an account if funds are short.
text:
Recognize it when: you miss bill due dates and pay late fees, or paying bills feels like a monthly emergency.
Technique: set the system up once, so paying bills needs little memory.
How: 1. List every bill with its due date.
2. Put each on a calendar as a monthly repeat, with reminders such as a week and two days before.
3. Use auto-pay for fixed bills if your income is steady, and check you will have enough money in the account that day, to avoid overdraft.
4. Or pay all bills in one sitting on a set day, such as payday, covering the next pay period.
5. Tick bills off on a simple checklist or spreadsheet so you can see what is still outstanding.
6. If it is an option, ask a partner to take over some payments.
Why it helps: it replaces remembering each due date with a one-time setup, and ticking bills off gives a clear picture.
Try saying: Future me will thank me for setting this up once.
If it does not work: start with the one bill you miss most often.

title: When you forget something, find which stage failed
source_document: Karidi, D. Remembering the Future: How ADHD Affects Prospective Memory. Attention Magazine (CHADD), Dec 2025
source_citation: Practitioner article by an ADHD coach and memory researcher in CHADD's magazine, with a reading list but no inline citations. The five-stage description is an explanation, not a tested tool.
text:
Recognize it when: you keep forgetting things you meant to do and feel it is just a bad memory.
Technique: work out where in the chain the plan broke, then fix that one stage.
How: 1. Encoding: did you actually store the plan, or did something interrupt you as you heard it? Fix: write it down at once.
2. Holding it: did it fade while you were busy? Fix: put it somewhere you will see it later.
3. Noticing the cue: did the moment come and you did not notice? Fix: make the cue louder or tie it to an event.
4. Doing it: did you remember but not act? Fix: shrink the first step to something tiny.
5. Checking: did you do it but wonder later? Fix: tick it off somewhere right after.
Why it helps: remembering the future takes five steps, so a slip at any one looks like forgetting. Naming the stage points to a fix and replaces blame with problem-solving.
Try saying: Which step failed this time: storing it, holding it, noticing the cue, doing it, or checking it?
If it does not work: if the same stage fails every time, ask a coach or clinician for help designing a support for it.

title: Make the reminder distinct, personal and in more than one place
source_document: Karidi, D. Remembering the Future: How ADHD Affects Prospective Memory. Attention Magazine (CHADD), Dec 2025
source_citation: Practitioner article in CHADD's magazine. The tips are the author's suggestions, not trial results.
text:
Recognize it when: your reminders fade into the background, such as a standard alarm you always swipe away.
Technique: make the cue impossible to miss and meaningful to you, and use more than one.
How: 1. Pick a cue that stands out: a special alarm tone, a bright sticky note on the door, an object in your shoe or on your keys.
2. Make it personal: for a call to your mum, use a song that reminds you of her.
3. Pair a phone reminder with a physical note, so it shows up in two places.
4. Use location reminders where available, such as a buzz when you pass the pharmacy.
5. Link the task to something visual, emotional or at a set place: bills at the same desk with the same playlist.
Why it helps: a plain alarm becomes background noise. A cue that is unusual, personal and in more than one place is harder to ignore.
Try saying: If it can fade, I make it louder or put it in a second place.
If it does not work: change the cue every few weeks, because even strong cues get ignored with time.

title: Body doubling and a text from a friend can carry follow-through
source_document: Karidi, D. Remembering the Future: How ADHD Affects Prospective Memory. Attention Magazine (CHADD), Dec 2025
source_citation: Practitioner article in CHADD's magazine. Described as support the author uses with clients, not as a tested treatment.
text:
Recognize it when: you plan to do something but keep not starting, or you stay on track only when someone is around.
Technique: work alongside another person, or let someone know your plan so they can nudge you.
How: 1. Pick the task and a time. Ask someone to be present in person or on a video call while you work on your own task.
2. Or make the plan visible: tell a friend 'I will walk at 6' and ask them to text 'ready for our walk?'.
3. Keep it light. The other person does not have to do anything but be there or check in.
4. A coach or therapist can also give structure for planning and tracking progress.
Why it helps: another person's presence adds gentle pressure and cuts distraction, and a check-in works as a reminder from outside your head.
Try saying: Can you sit with me for 20 minutes while I do this?
If it does not work: if you feel judged, choose someone who is calm and not invested in the result, or use a virtual coworking room.

title: Did you actually reply? Check, because you may have only answered in your head
source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD, drawing on his own experience. It cites one study on messages opened at a bad time (not verified here).
text:
Recognize it when: you are sure you replied, but the other person is still waiting, or you answered in your head and never sent it.
Technique: look at the thread and set a daily reminder to check whether the important ones were really sent.
How: 1. Open the message thread and check that your reply is there, not just in your head.
2. Set a daily reminder to scan messages from the people who matter most.
3. If you cannot answer now, leave the message unopened until you can, so it does not look dealt with.
4. Reply right away if you already know what to say.
Why it helps: opening a message at a bad moment makes the alert disappear, and a reply written only in your head feels done. A set check catches both.
Try saying: I will check the thread, not trust that I replied.
If it does not work: if you often leave replies half-written, send a short one now and add detail later.

title: Set a time to reply to messages and cut the alerts that bury them
source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD. Strategies are suggestions from experience.
text:
Recognize it when: messages pile up, you feel overwhelmed by the buzzing, or you avoid your phone because of it.
Technique: reply in a scheduled slot and keep only the alerts that matter.
How: 1. Pick a daily slot to read and answer messages together.
2. Keep a sticky note by your workspace listing who you need to text before the end of the day.
3. Turn off notification permissions for non-essential apps, so texts and email are not buried.
4. If a long reply feels heavy, send a quick voice message or make a call instead.
Why it helps: an inbox that buzzes all day causes overwhelm, and giving up on all of it is a common response. A fixed slot plus fewer alerts makes the job smaller.
Try saying: I answer messages at 5, and only the important apps get to buzz.
If it does not work: if the slot gets skipped, attach it to an existing routine such as after dinner.

title: Replied far too late? Send a short reply instead of avoiding it
source_document: Inflow: Texting with ADHD, 6 ways to stop ghosting your friends (Quentin Görres, Oct 27, 2022)
source_citation: Practitioner source: a company blog post by a freelance writer with ADHD. The 'shame cycle' claim cites a source not verified here.
text:
Recognize it when: you have not replied to a friend for days, and the longer it gets the harder it feels to answer.
Technique: break the shame cycle with a short, imperfect reply.
How: 1. Remind yourself it is probably a text, and the other person is not holding their breath.
2. Write one or two lines. A simple 'sorry for the slow reply, how are you?' is enough.
3. Skip the long explanation and the perfect GIF.
4. Send it before you start the next task.
Why it helps: avoidance, then anxiety, then guilt and shame can feed more avoidance. A short reply stops the loop and is usually received better than silence.
Try saying: Late and short beats perfect and never.
If it does not work: if you cannot face typing, use a voice message or a quick call.

title: Missed a deadline: tell your manager within the hour
source_document: ADHD Planner blog: I Missed a Deadline at Work Because of ADHD. Now What? (Ravi Mishra)
source_citation: Practitioner source: an ADHD planner app's blog by a writer who says it is personal experience, not medical advice. It cites a 2026 systematic review linking ADHD symptoms and procrastination, with mostly cross-sectional studies. The page promotes its own app; the method does not depend on it.
text:
Recognize it when: a deadline is slipping or has passed and you want to hide until it is done.
Technique: tell your manager early with a new date you can meet and what they will get first.
How: 1. Message them before they have to ask, so they can adjust their own plans.
2. Use three parts: what is late, what they get and when, and a short apology. For example: 'The report due today isn't ready. You'll have the summary section by 3 and the full draft tomorrow at noon. Sorry for the slip.'
3. Pick a new date you are confident you can beat.
4. Then list what is left in pieces small enough to finish in one sitting, with rough times. Double the time on anything new.
5. Close everything that is not this task, including your inbox, and do the piece you promised first.
Why it helps: early notice lets others adapt, and shrinking the work from one wall to pieces makes starting possible.
Try saying: It's late. Here is what you get and when. Sorry for the slip.
If it does not work: you do not have to say why. If misses keep happening, ask about accommodations, which is when a medical reason becomes relevant.

title: After a missed deadline, find where it slipped
source_document: ADHD Planner blog: I Missed a Deadline at Work Because of ADHD. Now What? (Ravi Mishra)
source_citation: Practitioner source: an ADHD planner app's blog, personal experience not medical advice. The three causes are the author's categories.
text:
Recognize it when: you finished the late work and want to stop it happening again.
Technique: ask which of three things went wrong, and fix only that one.
How: 1. Started too late: the work would have fit but began the day before. Make your own earlier deadlines inside the project.
2. Bigger than it looked: the estimate was off. Break the project into steps on day one and time the first two.
3. The date fell out of view: you knew, then it was nowhere you looked. Set a reminder a few days ahead, attached to the first step as well as the due date.
4. Write down which one it was, so patterns show over time.
Why it helps: each cause needs a different fix, and checking it once is quicker than guessing. One miss is a bad week; a pattern is worth a conversation.
Try saying: Which was it: late start, bigger than it looked, or lost date?
If it does not work: if it keeps happening, talk to your manager about accommodations such as written instructions, task lists and reminders.

title: Ask once for a standing adjustment instead of begging for each extension
source_document: Assignment Help Center: Deadline Extensions for ADHD & Dyslexia (Jun 22, 2026)
source_citation: LOW-TRUST source. The page is on a site that sells essay-writing services, so it has a commercial interest. Its order-data statistics were NOT used. Only the general idea (a documented, recurring accommodation via a university disability office) was used. Rules vary by country and institution, so check the university's own policy.
text:
Recognize it when: you ask tutors for a few extra days again and again and dread re-explaining yourself.
Technique: register with the disability or student support service early so an adjustment is documented once.
How: 1. Contact the disability or accessibility service at the start of a term, not the night before a deadline.
2. Bring evidence if you have it, such as a diagnosis or letter from a clinician. If you have none yet, ask what interim support is possible.
3. Describe the real impact, for example 'planning and sequencing take me far longer', not just 'I struggle'.
4. Ask for the agreed adjustment to be written into your support plan and confirmed in writing, and review it each year.
5. Use extra time on planning: break each task into stages.
Why it helps: a documented plan means you do not re-justify yourself under stress. It changes your timeline, not the standard the work is marked against.
Try saying: I would like an ongoing adjustment, recorded in my plan.
If it does not work: if it is delayed or refused, ask for the reason in writing, escalate within the service, and keep records. Do not pay anyone to write your work.
